glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: In parables by the sea, Jesus explains how people receive the word of the kingdom, how the kingdom grows amid opposition until the final harvest, and why it is worth everything; then His hometown takes offense at Him.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Matthew 13 is the third of Matthew’s great discourses. After the rejection in chapter 12, Jesus teaches the crowds from a boat and explains the parables to His disciples in the house.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “But he who received seed on the good ground is he who hears the word and understands it, who indeed bears fruit and produces: some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.’” (Matthew 13:23)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
The chapter opens with a sower, and Jesus Himself explains the story. The seed is the word of the kingdom, and the soils are the hearers: some lose the word to the evil one, some receive it with shallow joy and fall away under pressure, some let cares and riches choke it, and some understand and bear fruit. The same soils can describe different areas of one disciple’s heart, so the parable presses every hearer to receive Jesus’ word, not just to sort others.

The parables that follow describe a kingdom that is present but not yet complete. Wheat and tares grow together in the world until the Son of Man sends His angels at the end of the age. A tiny mustard seed becomes a tree where the birds of the air nest, a picture of the nations finding shelter under Christ’s reign, and leaven quietly works through the whole lump. A man finds a treasure and in his joy sells all he has, and a merchant sells everything for one pearl. Both pictures call for joyful, wholehearted surrender to the kingdom’s worth. The dragnet keeps final judgment in view. Then Nazareth, admiring His wisdom yet offended at His familiar family, shows unreceptive soil in a single town.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Matthew 13:1–9 — The Parable of the Sower

Jesus tells of seed falling on the wayside, stony places, thorns, and good ground, where it yields a crop of a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold. He calls those who have ears to hear.

Matthew 13:10–17 — Why Jesus Speaks in Parables

Jesus explains that the mysteries of the kingdom are given to His disciples, while those who refuse to see and hear fulfill Isaiah’s words. The disciples are blessed to see and hear what prophets longed for.

Matthew 13:18–23 — The Sower Explained

Jesus explains the sower: the seed is the word of the kingdom, and the soils show what keeps it from bearing fruit. The good ground is the one who hears, understands, and bears fruit.

Matthew 13:24–30 — The Parable of the Wheat and the Tares

An enemy sows tares among a man’s wheat, and the owner lets both grow together until the harvest, when the reapers will separate them.

Matthew 13:31–35 — The Mustard Seed, the Leaven, and Speaking in Parables

The kingdom is like a mustard seed that grows into a tree sheltering birds, and like leaven that works through the whole lump. Matthew notes that Jesus’ use of parables fulfills Psalm 78:2.

Matthew 13:36–43 — The Wheat and the Tares Explained

In the house Jesus explains the wheat and tares. The Son of Man sows good seed in the world, the devil sows the tares, and at the end of the age the angels will gather out the wicked, while the righteous shine in the Father’s kingdom.

Matthew 13:44–46 — The Hidden Treasure and the Pearl of Great Price

A man finds treasure hidden in a field and for joy sells all he has to buy it, and a merchant sells all he has for one pearl of great price. Both show the kingdom’s surpassing worth.

Matthew 13:47–52 — The Dragnet and the Householder’s Treasure

A dragnet gathers every kind of fish, and the bad are thrown away, as the angels will separate the wicked from the just. A scribe instructed concerning the kingdom brings out treasures new and old.

Matthew 13:53–58 — Rejected in His Hometown

In Nazareth the people marvel at Jesus’ wisdom and works yet are offended because they know His family. He does few mighty works there because of their unbelief.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Matthew 13 explains why the same message produces such different results. The seed is good; the difference lies in the hearer’s heart, and the soils invite honest cultivation of one’s own heart.

The chapter also teaches patience and hope. The kingdom begins small and hidden, grows past every expectation, and works from within until it changes everything it touches. Evil and good grow side by side for now, but the Son of Man will make the final separation. Meanwhile the kingdom is worth more than anything a person could give up to have it, and those who find it give joyfully. That surrender also echoes the King, who gave all to purchase His people (1 Corinthians 6:20).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Hearing the word. The soils show how the word of the kingdom is received or resisted (13:3–9, 18–23).

Revealing and concealing. Parables open the mysteries to disciples and hide them from willful refusal (13:11–15).

Growth amid resistance. The kingdom grows alongside evil until the harvest (13:24–33).

Surpassing worth. The treasure and the pearl call for joyful, total surrender (13:44–46).

Final separation. The harvest and the dragnet keep judgment in view (13:40–43, 49–50).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Parable (13:3). A story drawn from ordinary life that teaches about the kingdom. Jesus’ parables both reveal and conceal.

Mysteries of the kingdom (13:11). Truths about God’s reign once hidden and now revealed by God to Jesus’ disciples.

Tares (13:25). Weeds that look like wheat while growing. Jesus identifies them as the sons of the wicked one sown by the devil (13:38–39).

Mustard seed (13:31). A very small seed that grows into a large plant. The birds in its branches recall Ezekiel 17:22–24 and Daniel 4:12, where nations shelter under a great tree.

Leaven (13:33). Yeast that spreads quietly through dough. Here it pictures the reign of Christ working from within until it reaches the whole.

Things new and old (13:52). The instructed scribe holds together the Scriptures already given and their fulfillment now revealed in Jesus.

focus: Matthew 13 records the third of Jesus’ major discourses, a series of kingdom parables spoken to the multitudes by the sea, together with Jesus’ answer to His disciples about why He speaks in parables, followed by further explanation and parables given to the disciples in the house. Through the sower, the wheat and tares, the mustard seed, the leaven, the hidden treasure, the pearl, and the dragnet, Jesus explains why people respond to the kingdom word so differently, how the kingdom grows until the final separation at the end of the age, and why it is worth everything, and the chapter closes as His hometown of Nazareth takes offense at Him.

sections.title: The Parable of the Sower
sections.summary: Sitting in a boat while great multitudes stand on the shore, Jesus tells of a sower whose seed falls by the wayside, on stony places, among thorns, and on good ground. Only the seed on good ground yields a crop, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty, and Jesus says, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear!” (Matthew 13:9).

sections.title: Why Jesus Speaks in Parables
sections.summary: When the disciples ask why He speaks in parables, Jesus answers that it has been given to them to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but not to those who see without seeing and hear without hearing, in whom Isaiah’s prophecy is fulfilled. He tells the disciples that their eyes and ears are blessed, for many prophets and righteous men desired to see and hear what they see and hear.

sections.title: The Sower Explained
sections.summary: Jesus explains that the seed is the word of the kingdom: the wicked one snatches away what was sown by the wayside, the one on stony places receives it with joy but has no root in himself and stumbles when tribulation or persecution arises because of the word, and the cares of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word among the thorns. The good ground is the one who hears the word and understands it, and he bears fruit.

sections.title: The Parable of the Wheat and the Tares
sections.summary: Jesus likens the kingdom of heaven to a man who sows good seed in his field, but an enemy sows tares among the wheat while men sleep. The owner tells his servants to let both grow together until the harvest, when the reapers will gather the tares to be burned and the wheat into his barn.

sections.title: The Mustard Seed, the Leaven, and Speaking in Parables
sections.summary: Jesus likens the kingdom of heaven to a mustard seed, the least of all seeds, which grows into a tree where the birds of the air nest, and to leaven that a woman hides in three measures of meal until it is all leavened. Matthew adds that Jesus spoke all these things to the multitude in parables, fulfilling the prophet’s word, “I will open My mouth in parables” (Matthew 13:35).

sections.title: The Wheat and the Tares Explained
sections.summary: In the house Jesus explains that He, the Son of Man, sows the good seed, the field is the world, the good seeds are the sons of the kingdom, the tares are the sons of the wicked one, the enemy is the devil, and the harvest is the end of the age. At that harvest the Son of Man will send out His angels to gather all who practice lawlessness into the furnace of fire, and the righteous will shine forth as the sun in their Father’s kingdom.

sections.title: The Hidden Treasure and the Pearl of Great Price
sections.summary: Jesus likens the kingdom of heaven to treasure hidden in a field, which a man finds and, for joy over it, sells all that he has to buy that field. He likens it also to a merchant who finds one pearl of great price and sells all that he has to buy it.

sections.title: The Dragnet and the Householder’s Treasure
sections.summary: Jesus likens the kingdom of heaven to a dragnet that gathers fish of every kind, from which the good are kept and the bad thrown away, and He says the angels will likewise separate the wicked from among the just at the end of the age. When the disciples say they have understood, He tells them that every scribe instructed concerning the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old.

sections.title: Rejected in His Hometown
sections.summary: When Jesus has finished these parables, He goes to His own country and teaches in their synagogue, and the people are astonished at His wisdom and mighty works yet take offense at Him as the carpenter’s son. Jesus says, “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his own house” (Matthew 13:57), and He does not do many mighty works there because of their unbelief.
